Project Brief

The course project thread is a single Tic-Tac-Toe codebase carried across every module: versioned in Lab 1, kept clean and conflict-free in Lab 2, branched in Lab 3, unit-tested in Lab 4, and put behind an automated test pipeline in Lab 5, before teams extend it in the final project.

Module 1 · Lecture · Class 1

Intro to CI/CD & DevOps

What the pipeline is, why it exists, and the tools we will use to build one.

Modern software is rarely written once and shipped once. It is changed constantly, by many people, and each change has to be integrated, built, tested, and delivered without breaking what already works. DevOps is the culture and set of practices that make this fast and reliable; CI/CD is the automation at its heart.

Key ideas

DevOps

A way of working that unites development (writing code) and operations (building, testing, releasing, running) so that software moves from a developer's machine to its users smoothly and repeatedly. The goals are short feedback loops, automation of repetitive steps, and shared responsibility for quality.

Continuous Integration (CI)

Every change is merged into a shared repository frequently, and each merge automatically triggers a build and a set of tests. If a change breaks the build or fails a test, the team finds out within minutes instead of weeks. CI is the antidote to "integration hell," where code that worked in isolation collapses when combined.

Continuous Delivery / Deployment (CD)

CD extends CI: once a change passes all checks, the system automatically prepares it for release (delivery) or even releases it (deployment). The payoff is that shipping becomes a routine, low-risk button-press rather than a stressful manual event.

The pipeline, end to end

A CI/CD pipeline is an automated sequence that runs on every change:

source control  →  test  →  integrate  →  deliver

This course builds each stage from the ground up, and the last lab wires them together into a working pipeline.

The toolchain we will use

  • Git: the version-control system that records every change to the code.
  • Gitee (码云): our remote host for repositories, pull requests, issue tracking, and CI/CD. We use Gitee because it is fast and reliable from within China, where GitHub access is often slow or unstable.
  • Python 3 + pytest: to run the project and check it with automated tests in a structured, repeatable way.
  • Gitee Go: Gitee's built-in CI/CD service, which runs our build and tests automatically on every push.
Course project

Everything is taught around one small program: a console Tic-Tac-Toe game in Python. It starts as a single file you version with Git, gains a suite of automated tests, and finishes as a repository whose every commit is automatically tested by Gitee Go.

Glossary to remember

  • Repository (repo): a project tracked by Git, including its full history.
  • Commit: a recorded snapshot of changes, with a message.
  • Branch: an independent line of development.
  • Merge: combining the work of two branches.
  • Pipeline: the automated build/test/deliver sequence.
  • Unit test: a small automated check that one piece of code behaves correctly.
  • Artifact: a file produced by the pipeline (e.g. a test report or a packaged release).

DevOps technology & tools

Every stage of the loop is backed by a category of technology, and each category has many tools. A typical DevOps toolchain looks like this:

StageTechnology / purposeExample tools
PlanPlanning & issue trackingJira, Trello, Gitee / GitLab Issues
CodeSource control & editorsGit, VS Code, Gitee / GitLab / GitHub
BuildCompiling & build systemsMake, CMake, Maven, Gradle
TestAutomated testingpytest, unittest, JUnit, Jest, Selenium
ReleaseCI/CD orchestrationGitee Go, Jenkins, GitLab CI, GitHub Actions
DeployDeployment & containersDocker, Kubernetes, Ansible
OperateInfrastructure & configurationKubernetes, Ansible, Terraform
MonitorMonitoring & loggingPrometheus, Grafana, ELK Stack, Nagios

No team uses all of these: the point is that every stage can be automated, and the tools are what wire the stages into one continuous loop.

In this course

We use a small, self-contained slice of this toolchain: Git + Gitee (Plan & Code), pytest (Test), and Gitee Go (Release / CI). Containerised deploy-and-operate tools such as Docker and Kubernetes are powerful next steps beyond this short course.

Module 1 · Setup Lab · Class 2

Setup Lab: Get Your Machine Ready

Install and verify the full toolchain. Nothing later works until this does, so finish every checkpoint.

Goal

By the end of this lab you have a working Python toolchain, a Gitee account with SSH access, and you have successfully pushed a small program to a Gitee repository.

Before you start

Work through the steps in order: each builds on the last. Instructions focus on Windows (most common here) with short notes for macOS and Linux. Every tool has an official download link plus a China mirror in case the official one is slow.

1 · Install Git

Git is the version-control tool at the centre of the course. On Windows the installer also gives you Git Bash: the terminal you'll use throughout.

⇣ Git for Windows All platforms
Windows
  1. Download and run the installer from the link above.
  2. Accept the default option on every screen: the defaults are correct for this course. Keep "Git from the command line and also from 3rd-party software" selected.
  3. Finish, then open Git Bash from the Start menu.
Official download slow? Get Git for Windows from the Tsinghua mirror: mirrors.tuna.tsinghua.edu.cn/github-release/git-for-windows/git/
macOS / Linux

macOS: Git arrives with the Xcode Command Line Tools (Step 2). Linux: sudo apt install git on Debian/Ubuntu.

Then set your identity once, in any terminal:

git --version
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

2 · Install Python 3

You need Python 3 (3.10 or newer). On Windows, install it from python.org and be sure to add it to your PATH.

Windows
⇣ python.org/downloads
  1. Download the latest Windows installer (64-bit) from the link.
  2. Run it and, on the first screen, tick "Add python.exe to PATH" before clicking Install Now. This is the step people forget; without it the python command isn't found.
  3. Close and reopen Git Bash so the new PATH takes effect.
macOS / Linux

macOS: brew install python, or use the python.org installer. Linux: sudo apt install python3 python3-pip. On macOS/Linux the commands are usually python3 and pip3.

Verify in a fresh terminal (both the interpreter and its package installer, pip):

python --version
pip --version

If python isn't found on Windows, reopen the terminal; if it still fails, re-run the installer and confirm "Add python.exe to PATH" was ticked. On macOS/Linux use python3/pip3.

3 · Install pytest (the test runner)

pytest is the testing framework used from Module 5 onward. It installs with pip, Python's package manager, which came with Python in Step 2:

pip install pytest
In China, PyPI can be slow. Use the Tsinghua mirror: pip install -i https://pypi.tuna.tsinghua.edu.cn/simple pytest (or set it as your default, per the Tsinghua PyPI guide).

Verify:

pytest --version

If pytest isn't found directly, run it via the module form python -m pytest --version (and use pip3/python3 on macOS/Linux).

4 · Install VS Code & the Python extension

VS Code is the editor. Install it, then add Microsoft's Python extension from inside VS Code.

⇣ code.visualstudio.com
  1. Download and install VS Code for your operating system.
  2. Open VS Code → click the Extensions icon in the left bar (or press Ctrl+Shift+X).
  3. Search for and install Python (by Microsoft); it bundles Pylance plus run/debug and test support.
Tip

The first time you run a Python file, VS Code may ask which interpreter to use: choose the Python 3 you installed in Step 2 (Command Palette with Ctrl+Shift+P → Python: Select Interpreter).

5 · Create a Gitee account & SSH key

Gitee hosts your repositories and runs the CI pipeline. To push your commits up to Gitee, your computer has to prove who it is every time it connects. There are two ways to do that, HTTPS and SSH, and it is worth understanding the difference before you set one up.

HTTPS vs. SSH: two ways to authenticate

Both transport the exact same Git data; they only differ in how the server checks that the connection is allowed.

HTTPSSSH
Remote URL looks likehttps://gitee.com/user/repo.gitgit@gitee.com:user/repo.git
How you prove it's youUsername + password / access token, typed (or cached) on each push.A cryptographic key pair stored once on your machine, no password typed.
Setup effortNone up front, but you re-enter credentials (or manage a token) repeatedly.A few minutes once; after that, pushing is friction-free.
Best whenOne-off clones, machines you don't control, networks that block SSH.Your own daily-driver machine, which is our case.

We use SSH in this course: you set it up once and never type a password to push again.

How SSH keys work

SSH uses a matched key pair: a private key that stays secret on your computer, and a public key you give to Gitee. When you connect, Gitee challenges your machine to prove it holds the matching private key, without the private key ever leaving your computer. The public key is safe to share; the private key (the file without .pub) must never be copied or posted anywhere.

↗ Register on gitee.com
  1. Create and verify an account at gitee.com.
  2. In Git Bash, generate a key pair (press Enter at every prompt to accept the defaults): 
    ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com"

    Breaking the command down:

    • ssh-keygen: the program that creates a new SSH key pair.
    • -t ed25519: the key type (algorithm). Ed25519 is the modern, fast, secure default.
    • -C "you@example.com": a comment label attached to the key so you can recognise it later in Gitee's list. It does not have to be a real email; it's just a tag.

    This writes two files into ~/.ssh/: id_ed25519 (your private key, keep secret) and id_ed25519.pub (your public key, safe to share). The prompts ask where to save it (Enter = default) and for an optional passphrase that encrypts the private key on disk.

  3. Display and copy the public key: note the .pub extension; never copy the other file: 
    cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

    cat prints a file's contents to the screen. Select the whole line it outputs (it starts with ssh-ed25519 and ends with your comment) and copy it.

  4. On Gitee: avatar → Settings → SSH Public Keys → Add Public Key → paste it and save. This tells Gitee to trust any machine that holds the matching private key.
  5. Test the connection: 
    ssh -T git@gitee.com

    ssh opens a secure connection; -T skips requesting an interactive terminal (Gitee doesn't offer a shell, only Git); git@gitee.com is the user git on the host gitee.com. A successful run greets you by your username: that confirms your key is recognised.

First-connection prompt

The first time you run ssh -T, you'll see "The authenticity of host 'gitee.com' can't be established… continue connecting (yes/no)?", type yes. This records Gitee's fingerprint so future connections are trusted automatically.

"Does not provide shell access" is success

A correct test prints something like "Hi user(@user)! You've successfully authenticated, but GITEE.COM does not provide shell access." That is not an error. The first half means your key worked and Gitee knows who you are. The second half is normal: the git account exists only to handle push/pull, not to give you a command prompt, so it logs you out instead of opening a shell (which is why we pass -T). A real failure looks different: Permission denied (publickey).

6 · Smoke test (the checkpoint)

Prove the whole toolchain works end-to-end. First, pick a folder to work in and create the file you'll run.

  1. Choose a home for your project: somewhere easy to find, not inside a synced folder like OneDrive or Desktop. A path with no spaces or non-English characters avoids headaches later. For example: 
    # create the folder and move into it
mkdir -p ~/dev/hello
cd ~/dev/hello

    mkdir -p ~/dev/hello makes a dev/hello folder in your home directory (-p creates parents as needed and won't complain if it already exists); cd moves your terminal into that folder, so every command after this runs there.

  2. Create hello.py in this folder. Either run the echo command in the block below, or, if you prefer, open the folder in VS Code (code .) and create hello.py by hand with the same contents.
  3. Create the remote repository on Gitee so you have somewhere to push to. On gitee.com: + (top-right) → New Repository. Set Repository name to hello, and, importantly, leave it empty: do not tick "Initialize this repository", and don't add a README, .gitignore, or licence. An empty repo lets your local commits push cleanly without conflicts. Click Create.
This folder is your workspace

The folder you just made is your local workspace: the actual files on your disk that you edit and run. When you run git init below, Git starts tracking changes inside this folder. How a file moves from your workspace all the way to Gitee (workspace → staging → local repo → remote) is the core of the next class, so don't worry about the git commands' details yet: just run them and watch it work.

Now run the full sequence from inside that folder:

# write and run a hello program
echo 'print("toolchain OK")' > hello.py
python hello.py

# version it and push to a new empty Gitee repo
git init
git add hello.py
git commit -m "first commit: hello"
git remote add origin git@gitee.com:<your-user>/hello.git
git push -u origin master

Replace <your-user> (brackets and all) with your Gitee username: the handle from the "Hi user(@user)!" message in the SSH test. Easiest of all: open the new repo on Gitee → green Clone button → SSH tab → copy the exact git@gitee.com:… URL and paste it in place of the one above.

Done when

You can run python hello.py, and hello.py appears in your repository on the Gitee website.

Module 2 · Lecture · Class 3

Git Basics

How Git tracks your work across four locations: the mental model behind Lab 1.

Git is a version-control system: it records snapshots of your project over time so you can review history, undo mistakes, and collaborate without overwriting each other's work. The key to using it confidently is understanding where a file lives at any moment.

The four locations

Every change moves through four places. Today's lab is built entirely around tracking files across them:

  • Workspace (working directory): the actual files you edit on disk.
  • Staging Area (index): a holding area for changes you have marked to include in the next commit.
  • Local Repository: the committed history stored on your own machine.
  • Remote Repository: the shared copy on Gitee that your team pulls from and pushes to.

The core commands

Use this block as a quick map of which command moves a change between which two locations, then read the detail below for when and how to reach for each one.

git clone <url>     # copy a remote repo to your workspace
git status          # what changed, and where it lives now
git add <file>       # workspace  → staging area
git reset           # staging area → workspace (unstage)
git commit          # staging area → local repository
git push            # local repo  → remote repository
git pull            # remote repo → local + workspace
git log             # view commit history
git diff            # view exact changes

The examples below all use the hello repository you pushed to Gitee in the Setup Lab smoke test (git@gitee.com:adasuper/hello.git, swap in your own username). Imagine you are coming back to it on a fresh machine to make a small change.

git clone <url>

When: once per project, to make a local copy of a repository that already exists on Gitee.

How: run it in the folder where you want the project to land. It creates a new sub-folder, downloads the full history, and wires up the remote (named origin) for you, so git init + git remote add are unnecessary.

Example: grab your hello repo onto a new machine and step into it:

git clone git@gitee.com:adasuper/hello.git
cd hello

git status

When: constantly, before and after almost every other command. It is your map of where each file currently lives.

How: it needs no arguments and changes nothing; it lists files that are modified but unstaged, files staged for the next commit, and files Git isn't tracking yet.

Example: after editing hello.py to print a friendlier message:

git status
# Changes not staged for commit:
#   modified:   hello.py

git add <file>

When: after editing, to mark exactly which changes belong in your next commit (workspace → staging).

How: name specific files to stage them deliberately, or use . to stage everything changed. Staging is what lets you commit two edits separately even if you made them at the same time.

Example: stage your edited hello.py:

git add hello.py         # just this file
git add .                  # everything changed in the hello folder

git reset <file>

When: you staged something by mistake and want to take it back out of the next commit (staging → workspace).

How: it unstages the file while keeping your edits: your file on disk is untouched, it just won't be in the next commit. It is the exact undo of git add (which is why Lab 1 has you add then unstage).

Example: you staged hello.py but realise you aren't done editing it:

git reset hello.py        # back to unstaged; your edits remain

git reset --soft vs git reset --hard

git reset can also rewind a whole commit by pointing the branch at an earlier one. The mode flag decides how far the undo reaches across the three locations, and this is where you can lose work, so understand it before using it.

  • --soft: moves the branch back, but keeps everything staged. The commit is undone; its changes sit ready in the staging area as if you'd just run git add. Use it to redo a commit message or fold several commits into one. Nothing is lost.
  • --mixed (the default, what you get with no flag): moves the branch back and unstages the changes, but leaves your edits in the workspace. This is the same family as the file-level git reset <file> above. Nothing is lost.
  • --hard: moves the branch back and throws away the changes in both the staging area and the workspace, resetting your files on disk to match the target commit. This permanently deletes uncommitted work: there is no undo.
git reset --soft HEAD~1    # undo last commit, keep changes staged
git reset HEAD~1           # (--mixed) undo last commit, keep changes in workspace
git reset --hard HEAD~1    # undo last commit AND discard the changes: careful!
Handle --hard with care

--hard is the only one of the three that destroys work you haven't committed. Reach for --soft or the default --mixed unless you are absolutely certain you want those edits gone. HEAD~1 means "one commit before the current tip"; HEAD~2 would go back two, and so on.

git commit -m "message"

When: once a staged set of changes forms one complete, logical unit of work (staging → local repository).

How: always include a clear message with -m. The commit is a permanent snapshot in your local history: it is not on Gitee yet until you push.

Example: record your greeting change as a commit:

git commit -m "print a friendlier greeting"

git push

When: after committing, to publish your local commits so teammates and the CI pipeline can see them (local → remote).

How: the first push of a new branch needs -u origin <branch> to link it; after that, a bare git push is enough.

Example: the smoke test already ran the first form, so from now on a bare push is all you need:

git push -u origin master    # first time (done in the smoke test)
git push                      # every push to hello after that

git pull (and git fetch)

When: before you start working, and whenever a teammate has pushed to hello, to bring their commits into your copy.

How: run it with a clean workspace (commit or stash your own changes first) to avoid merge conflicts. The distinction matters: git fetch only downloads new commits into your local repository (remote → local repo) and leaves your working files untouched, so you can inspect what changed first. git pull is fetch followed by merge: it goes one step further and updates the files on your disk too (remote → local repo → workspace).

Example: sync the hello repo before adding your next change:

git fetch                   # download new commits, hello.py on disk unchanged
git pull                    # download AND update hello.py on disk

git log

When: any time you need to see the history of a repository: what was changed, by whom, and when.

How: it lists past commits newest-first with author, date, and message. Add --oneline for a compact one-row-per-commit view.

Example: review the history of hello after your new commit:

git log --oneline
# a1b2c3d  print a friendlier greeting
# e4f5a6b  first commit: hello

git diff

When: to review the exact line-by-line changes you've made, typically right before git add or git commit.

How: git diff alone shows unstaged edits (workspace vs. staging); git diff --staged shows what's already staged for the next commit (staging vs. last commit).

Example: check what you changed in hello.py before staging it:

git diff                    # unstaged edits to hello.py
git diff --staged           # what the next commit will record

The journey of a change

You edit a file (workspace) → git add it (staging) → git commit it (local repo) → git push it (remote). Each command moves the change one step closer to being shared. Knowing which command moves a file between which two locations is the whole game, and the worksheet in Lab 1 makes you trace it explicitly.

Good habits

  • Commit small, logical units of work: not "everything at once."
    A commit that does one thing is easy to understand, and if it introduces a bug you can undo just that change without losing unrelated work. A giant "did lots of stuff" commit hides what actually happened and is painful to reverse.
  • Write clear messages: "add input prompt", not "stuff".
    Months later, the message is often the only clue to why a change was made. A good message lets you (and teammates) scan the history and find the right commit without reading every line of code.
  • Run git status often; it is your map.
    It tells you exactly which files are modified, staged, or untracked before you act. Checking first prevents the common mistakes of committing the wrong file or forgetting to stage one you meant to include.
  • Always git pull before you start working, and pull once more right before you push.
    Pulling first means you build on your teammates' latest work instead of an outdated copy. Pulling again just before pushing catches anything that landed while you were coding, so conflicts surface locally where they are easy to fix, rather than your push being rejected because the remote moved ahead.
  • Keep a useful README.md describing the project.
    It is the first thing anyone (including future you) reads to learn what the project does and how to build and run it. A clear README turns a pile of files into a project someone can actually pick up.

Going further

This lecture covers the handful of commands you need day to day. When you want the complete, authoritative reference for any Git command and its options, consult the official documentation:

The file you will track

When a step says to create tictactoe.py, paste the seed game below (a two-player hot-seat board; win detection arrives in Lab 2). For tracking purposes, write it in the table as tictactoe.py ("seed").

# tictactoe.py: seed (hot-seat, no win detection yet)

board = ['1', '2', '3', '4', '5', '6', '7', '8', '9']
player = 'X'
filled = 0


def draw():
    for r in range(3):
        print(f" {board[r*3]}|{board[r*3+1]}|{board[r*3+2]}")


while filled < 9:
    draw()
    cell = input(f"Player {player}, cell 1-9: ")

    if not cell.isdigit() or not (1 <= int(cell) <= 9) or board[int(cell) - 1] in ('X', 'O'):
        print("invalid")
        continue

    board[int(cell) - 1] = player
    filled += 1
    player = 'O' if player == 'X' else 'X'

draw()
print("Board full - draw (win detection in Lab 2)")

Module 3 · Lecture · Class 5a

Ignoring Files with .gitignore

Keeping machine-specific junk and regenerated artifacts out of the repository.

Why ignore files at all?

A repository should hold source, the files a human writes, and nothing that can be regenerated from that source or that only makes sense on one person's machine. Committing everything else causes four concrete problems:

  • Bloat. Generated caches and dependency folders are large or numerous and change constantly, inflating the repository and slowing down every clone.
  • Noise. Generated files flood git status and git diff, burying the real source changes you actually want to review.
  • Non-portability. A .pyc bytecode file is tied to your exact Python version, so it is useless to a teammate on a different setup, yet still downloaded on every pull.
  • Needless conflicts. Files that differ per machine (editor settings, build output) get rewritten by everyone, so they collide constantly, even though nobody meaningfully changed the project.

The fix is a .gitignore file: a list of patterns telling Git which paths to leave untracked. Crucially, .gitignore itself is committed, so the whole team automatically shares the same rules. A typical one for this course's Python project:

# .gitignore for a Python project
__pycache__/    # compiled-bytecode cache folders
*.pyc           # individual bytecode files
.pytest_cache/  # pytest's cache
.venv/          # virtual environment
.vscode/        # per-developer editor settings

What should you ignore?

A good rule of thumb: if a file can be regenerated, is specific to one machine, or should stay secret, ignore it. In practice the things you exclude fall into a few categories:

  • Generated and cached files. Anything Python or your tools produce from the source: the __pycache__/ bytecode-cache folders, *.pyc files, and .pytest_cache/.
  • Editor and IDE settings. Per-developer configuration that differs from machine to machine: .vscode/, JetBrains' .idea/, Vim swap files (*.swp).
  • Operating-system junk. Files the OS sprinkles into folders: .DS_Store on macOS, Thumbs.db on Windows.
  • Downloaded dependencies. Packages a tool can fetch again on demand, so there is no need to store them: e.g. a Python virtual environment .venv/, or node_modules/ in a JavaScript project.
  • Logs and temporary files. Throwaway output such as *.log and *.tmp.
  • Secrets and local-only config. Anything with passwords, API keys, or tokens: .env files, credential files. Never commit these, even by accident.

By contrast, you should always commit the things a teammate genuinely needs: your source files (*.py), the tests, the dependency list (requirements.txt), the README.md, and .gitignore itself. The test is simple: could a teammate re-create everything else from what's committed? If yes, the generated result doesn't belong in the repo.

A cautionary tale: committing .vscode/

It is tempting to git add . and commit everything, including the .vscode/ folder VS Code creates. Here is why that bites you. The folder holds machine-specific settings: for example each developer's .vscode/settings.json records the absolute path to their Python interpreter:

// Alice's .vscode/settings.json
{ "python.defaultInterpreterPath": "C:/Users/Alice/AppData/Local/Programs/Python/Python312/python.exe" }

// Bob's .vscode/settings.json (different machine!)
{ "python.defaultInterpreterPath": "/usr/local/bin/python3" }

Now watch what happens once that file is tracked:

  1. Alice opens the project; VS Code rewrites settings.json with her path. She commits and pushes it.
  2. Bob pulls, opens the project; VS Code immediately rewrites the same line with his path. He commits and pushes.
  3. Alice opens VS Code again the next day, it rewrites the line back to her path. She pushes…

The result is an endless tug-of-war: every teammate's editor keeps overwriting the same line, producing a merge conflict on a file that has nothing to do with the actual program. You waste time resolving conflicts in settings nobody cares about. Listing .vscode/ in .gitignore from the start avoids the whole mess: each person keeps their own local settings, untracked.

Already committed it?

.gitignore only stops Git from tracking files it is not already tracking. If .vscode/ (or a build artifact) is already committed, adding it to .gitignore does nothing until you stop tracking it explicitly:

git rm -r --cached .vscode   # untrack, but keep the files on disk
git commit -m "stop tracking editor settings"

.gitignore syntax in detail

Each non-blank line is one pattern. Patterns are matched relative to the location of the .gitignore file. The rules:

PatternMeaningExample match
# textA comment. Blank lines are ignored too, so you can group rules.n/a
notes.txtMatches a file or folder named notes.txt anywhere in the tree.notes.txt, src/notes.txt
__pycache__/Trailing / matches directories only (and everything inside).__pycache__/, not a file of that name
*.pyc* matches any run of characters except /. Great for extensions.board.pyc, game.pyc
/secret.txtA leading / anchors the pattern to the folder of the .gitignore, so only the root one matches.secret.txt at root, not sub/secret.txt
logs/**/*.log** matches across nested directories.logs/a/b/run.log
file?.txt? matches exactly one character.file1.txt, not file10.txt
*.log
!keep.log		! negates a pattern: it re-includes something a previous line excluded. (You cannot re-include a file if its parent folder is ignored.)ignores every .log except keep.log

Order matters for negation: a later ! line overrides an earlier ignore. For everything else, the patterns are simply a set.

Module 3 · Lecture · Class 5b

Resolving Merge Conflicts

What happens when two teammates edit the same lines, and how to reconcile them.

How a conflict arises

Git merges most parallel work automatically. A conflict happens only in one specific situation: two people change the same lines of the same file, based on the same starting point, and both try to share their version. Git cannot know which one is "right", so it stops and asks a human to decide.

Let's walk through it concretely with two teammates, Alice and Bob, who each cloned the same hello repository. Both start from the same commit, in which hello.py's greeting line reads:

print("toolchain OK")

Setup: add your teammate to the repository

For two people to push to the same repository, the owner must first grant the other access. A freshly created Gitee repo is private to its owner, so Bob couldn't push to Alice's hello repo until she adds him as a member. Here is how Alice (the owner) does it:

  1. Open the repository on gitee.com and click the Settings (管理) tab near the top of the repo page.
  2. In the left menu, choose Members (仓库成员管理), then the Developer (开发者) tab. Developers can push code; lower roles like Reporter are read-only and cannot push.
  3. Click Invite member by link (邀请链接) to generate an invitation link.
  4. Copy that link and send it to your teammate (chat, email, etc.).
  5. The teammate opens the link and clicks accept to join. The access only takes effect after they accept.

Once Bob has accepted the link, he can clone the repo over SSH and push to it just like Alice. With both teammates able to push, the stage is set for a conflict.

Roles at a glance

Owner and Admin/Master can manage the repo and its members; Developer can push code; Reporter can only read and open issues. For this exercise, both teammates need Developer or higher.

Step by step to the collision

Each step below tracks the greeting line as it sits in all five locations. Repo A is Alice's clone, Repo B is Bob's; a highlighted cell is what changed in that step. The starting point, just after both cloned:

Repo A WorkspaceRepo A Local RepositoryRemote RepositoryRepo B Local RepositoryRepo B Workspace
"toolchain OK"
"toolchain OK"
"toolchain OK"
"toolchain OK"
"toolchain OK"
  1. Both edit the same line. Independently, each rewrites the greeting to their own taste: 
    # Alice changes it to:
print("Hello, world!")

# Bob changes it to:
print("Hi there!")
    Repo A WorkspaceRepo A Local RepositoryRemote RepositoryRepo B Local RepositoryRepo B Workspace
    "Hello, world!"
    "toolchain OK"
    "toolchain OK"
    "toolchain OK"
    "Hi there!"
  2. Alice ships first. Her push succeeds because nobody else has pushed since she cloned: 
    # Alice (Repo A)
git add hello.py
git commit -m "reword the greeting"
git push                     # ✓ remote now has Alice's line
    Repo A WorkspaceRepo A Local RepositoryRemote RepositoryRepo B Local RepositoryRepo B Workspace
    "Hello, world!"
    "Hello, world!"
    "Hello, world!"
    "toolchain OK"
    "Hi there!"
  3. Bob's push is rejected. Bob committed locally too, but the remote moved ahead of him, so Git refuses the push: 
    # Bob (Repo B)
git add hello.py
git commit -m "shorten the greeting"
git push
# ! [rejected]  (non-fast-forward)
# Updates were rejected because the remote contains work you do
# not have locally. Integrate the remote changes before pushing.
    Repo A WorkspaceRepo A Local RepositoryRemote RepositoryRepo B Local RepositoryRepo B Workspace
    "Hello, world!"
    "Hello, world!"
    "Hello, world!"
    "Hi there!"
    "Hi there!"

    The push changed nothing on the remote (it was rejected), so Bob's commit lives only in his local repository, one step behind the remote.

  4. Bob pulls, and the conflict surfaces. The pull downloads Alice's commit and tries to merge it with Bob's. Because they touched the same line, Git can't auto-merge: 
    git pull
# Auto-merging hello.py
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in hello.py
# Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.

git status
# Unmerged paths:
#   both modified:   hello.py
    Repo A WorkspaceRepo A Local RepositoryRemote RepositoryRepo B Local RepositoryRepo B Workspace
    "Hello, world!"
    "Hello, world!"
    "Hello, world!"
    "Hi there!"
    ⚠ conflict (both)

    The merge isn't committed yet, so Bob's local repository still holds his own commit; only his workspace file now carries the conflict markers.

Reading the conflict markers

Git rewrites the conflicting region of hello.py in place, wrapping both versions in markers. Bob opens the file and sees:

<<<<<<< HEAD
  print("Hi there!")             # Bob's version (his local HEAD)
=======
  print("Hello, world!")         # Alice's version (from the remote)
>>>>>>> origin/master
  • <<<<<<< HEAD begins your side (Bob's current commit).
  • ======= divides the two versions.
  • >>>>>>> origin/master ends their side (the incoming commit).

Resolving it

  1. Edit the file to the single correct result, deleting all three marker lines. Bob talks to Alice and they agree on one wording: 
      print("Hello there!")

    In VS Code, the merge editor shows Accept Current / Accept Incoming / Accept Both buttons above the conflict, but you can always just type the final line by hand, which is often clearest.

    Repo A WorkspaceRepo A Local RepositoryRemote RepositoryRepo B Local RepositoryRepo B Workspace
    "Hello, world!"
    "Hello, world!"
    "Hello, world!"
    "Hi there!"
    "Hello there!"
  2. Mark it resolved by staging the file: 
    git add hello.py
    Repo A WorkspaceRepo A Local RepositoryRemote RepositoryRepo B Local RepositoryRepo B Workspace
    "Hello, world!"
    "Hello, world!"
    "Hello, world!"
    "Hi there!"
    "Hello there!"

    Staging records the resolved file in the index. None of these five locations change yet; that happens at the commit.

  3. Complete the merge with a commit describing what you reconciled, then push: 
    git commit -m "merged two changes"   # records the merge
git push                          # ✓ remote now has the reconciled line
    Repo A WorkspaceRepo A Local RepositoryRemote RepositoryRepo B Local RepositoryRepo B Workspace
    "Hello, world!"
    "Hello, world!"
    "Hello there!"
    "Hello there!"
    "Hello there!"

Finally, Alice runs git pull to receive the merged result cleanly, bringing every location into agreement:

Repo A WorkspaceRepo A Local RepositoryRemote RepositoryRepo B Local RepositoryRepo B Workspace
"Hello there!"
"Hello there!"
"Hello there!"
"Hello there!"
"Hello there!"

The takeaway from the previous lecture's habit holds: had Bob git pulled before starting, he'd have built on Alice's line and likely avoided the clash entirely. git status guides you the whole time: it always lists exactly which files remain unmerged.

Stuck mid-merge?

If a merge gets messy and you want to bail out and start over, git merge --abort returns you to the state just before the pull, nothing lost.

Module 4 · Lecture · Class 7

Git Branching

Diverging from the main line of development to work without interfering with it.

1 · What is branching?

Branching is not new in Git: almost every version-control system supports it. Branching means diverging from the main line of development and continuing to work without interfering with that main line.

Branches in Git are extremely lightweight. Think of a branch as nothing more than a movable pointer to a specific commit. Because there is no memory overhead, it is cheap and natural to use branches to logically divide your work. Creating one is instant; switching between them just changes which version of the files you see on disk.

Visualize it

As you read, try each action in the interactive branch playground, hosted locally so it works even when the original site is slow or blocked: open Learn Git Branching. Watching the pointers move is the fastest way to build intuition. This tool is the open-source Learn Git Branching by Peter Cottle, used here under the MIT license; all credit goes to the original author.

2 · When do you branch?

So far you have worked on a single branch (master). There are times when you need to temporarily diverge and work on a "separate project". Three common scenarios:

Keep development off the delivered system

You are adding new features to an already delivered system, and you want to make sure your ongoing work does not destabilise the version users depend on until it is ready.

Solution: keep a dev branch separate from master. Merge into master only when the new features are ready to ship.

Hot bug fix

You are mid-way through a new feature when QA reports a critical bug in already-released code that must be fixed immediately.

Solution: switch to master, create a bugfix branch from it, fix the bug, and merge it back into master. Then switch back to your feature branch and carry on, your unfinished work undisturbed.

Work in parallel

Several engineers share one project. The work is split and assigned to individuals who mostly work at the same time. Having everyone commit to one shared branch quickly gets messy.

Solution: each member creates their own task branch off dev. When a task is finished, it merges back into dev.

Notice the pattern

The word merge appears in every scenario. Branches usually represent short-lived work that exists only temporarily. As soon as a branch has served its purpose, merge it back and delete it. Leaving stale branches around (and not merging in time) is a common source of avoidable merge conflicts.

3 · Working with branches

The commands below are all you need day to day. The activities use your hello repository from the Setup Lab.

1) Create a branch: git branch <name>

  • Creates a new branch pointing at the current commit (it does not switch you to it).
  • Does not work if the parent branch is empty (has no commits yet).
Activity: create a dev branch and list branches 
# in a fresh folder
git clone git@gitee.com:adasuper/hello.git
cd hello
git branch dev          # create dev; you are STILL on master
git branch             # list local branches
#   dev
# * master                (the * and green mark the current branch)
git branch -a          # also show remote branches
#   dev
# * master
#   remotes/origin/HEAD -> origin/master
#   remotes/origin/master

Only origin/master shows up under remotes because you have not pushed the new dev branch yet. (More on remote branches below.)

2) Switch to a branch: git checkout <name>

  • Switches to the named branch and updates your workspace files to match it.
  • git switch <name> does exactly the same thing (newer, clearer syntax).
  • git checkout -b <name> creates and switches in one step.
Activity: switch to dev, then create-and-switch to testing 
git checkout dev        # Switched to branch 'dev'
git switch master         # same idea, switch back
git checkout -b testing  # create 'testing' and switch to it at once

3) Delete a branch: git branch -d <name>

  • Deletes the named local branch.
  • You cannot delete the branch you are currently on: switch away first.
  • You cannot delete a branch with unmerged changes (use -D to force, carefully).
Activity: delete the testing branch 
git checkout dev
git branch -d testing    # Deleted branch testing (was dfc0baa).

4) Merge a branch: git merge <name>

Merging brings another branch's work into the current branch. There are two outcomes:

Fast-forward. If master has not moved since you branched, Git just slides the master pointer forward to the tip of dev. No new commit is created.

# commit once on dev, then merge into master
git checkout dev
# create code.txt, then:
git add -A
git commit -m "added code.txt"
git checkout master
git merge dev            # Fast-forward

# before:   c0 - c1 - c2        master -> c1,  dev -> c2
# after:    c0 - c1 - c2        master -> c2,  dev -> c2   (pointer just moved)

Merge commit (three-way merge). If both branches gained commits since they diverged, Git creates a special merge commit with two parents that ties the histories together. This may require resolving a conflict, exactly as in Lab 2.

# commit on master AND on dev, then merge
# on master: modify code.txt, add, commit
git checkout dev
# create resource.txt, add, commit
git checkout master
git merge dev            # creates a merge commit

# before:        c3              master -> c3
#               /
#         c0 - c1 - c2 - c4     dev  -> c4
# after:         c3 ----- c5    c5 = merge commit (parents c3 and c4)
#               /        /
#         c0 - c1 - c2 - c4
Keep the feature branch fresh

After merging dev into master, also update dev so it includes the latest master, which avoids future conflicts: git checkout dev then git merge master.

5) Combine history with rebase: git rebase <name>

Rebasing is another way to combine work. It takes a set of commits, "copies" them, and replays them on top of the checked-out branch, producing a linear history instead of a merge commit.

Rebase rewrites history

Rebasing creates copies of commits; the originals are no longer reachable by their branch. On shared branches this can wipe out other people's work. Do not rebase unless you are 100% sure it is the right tool, and never rebase commits others have already pulled.

The typical local flow: fix a bug on a bugfix branch, rebase it onto master so the fix sits neatly after master's latest commit, resolve any conflict, then fast-forward master and delete the branch. For a deeper comparison see the reference link at the end.

6) Remote branches

So far everything has been local. A name like origin/master is a remote-tracking branch: the convention is <remote name>/<branch name>. It reflects the state of the remote as of your last pull or fetch.

Crucially, remote-tracking branches live in your local repository. Treat them as cached references to the real remote (they are sometimes called "upstreams"). They only update when you communicate with the remote.

7) Publish a new local branch: git push --set-upstream origin <name>

A plain git push only pushes the current branch, and only if it already has a remote counterpart. The first time you push a brand-new local branch, Git does not yet know where to send it:

git checkout dev
git push
# fatal: The current branch dev has no upstream branch.
# To push the current branch and set the remote as upstream, use
#     git push --set-upstream origin dev

The fix is given to you in the message. Running it creates origin/dev and links your local dev to it, so future pushes on dev are just git push:

git push --set-upstream origin dev   # or the short form: git push -u origin dev

8) Pull branches from the remote

When a teammate (or a second clone) has pushed work, you bring it in with git pull on the matching branch. A fresh git clone already captures information about all remote branches.

Activity: sync a change across two clones 
# in a second workspace, Repo2:
git clone git@gitee.com:adasuper/hello.git
git branch -a            # all branch info captured by the clone
# ... in Repo1, change dev, add, commit, push ...
# back in Repo2:
git checkout dev
git pull                 # receive Repo1's latest dev work
A cleaner way to see push and pull

Now that you understand remote branches: git pull is merging the remote branch into your local branch, and git push is merging your local branch into the remote branch.

9) Delete a remote branch: git push -d origin <name>

Deleting a branch locally (git branch -d task) leaves the remote copy in place. To remove it from the remote too:

git push -d origin task   # delete the remote branch origin/task

As always, trim short-lived branches once they have served their purpose to keep the repository tidy.

The Pull Request workflow on Gitee

On a team, you usually do not merge a feature branch yourself. Instead you open a Pull Request so the change can be reviewed first:

  1. Push your feature branch to Gitee (git push -u origin feature/x).
  2. Open a Pull Request (PR) proposing to merge it into master.
  3. A teammate reviews the changes and comments.
  4. Merge the PR, delete the branch, and everyone pulls the updated master.

PRs are where code review happens, and, once we add CI in Module 6, where automated tests gate the merge. PRs can also be linked to issues so that merging automatically closes the task it addressed.

References

  • Pro Git book (git-scm.com)
  • Learn Git Branching by Peter Cottle (interactive branch visualizer, MIT license): local copy · original site
  • Atlassian: merging vs. rebasing

Lab 3: Branching on the Tic-Tac-Toe Game

Two developers grow the game on a dev branch, fix a planted bug on a bugfix branch, and sync it back into master. For every step, record the Git command(s) and any non-Git operations.

Open this lab in a new tab first

Your worksheet answers are typed directly into this page and are not saved: navigating away (for example, back to the lecture notes) will erase everything you've entered. Before you start, right-click this page and choose "Open in new tab/window" (or Ctrl/Cmd + click a nav link) so you can read the lecture in one tab and keep your log safe in another. When you're done, use the print button to save a PDF.

Two developers, Alice and Ben, continue the Tic-Tac-Toe project from Lab 1. Its master branch already holds the tictactoe.py seed (hot-seat board, no win detection). On a shared dev branch each developer adds one real function to the game:

  • Alice adds check_win() for win detection. It ships with an intentional bug.
  • Ben adds board_full() for draw detection.

During play-testing the bug surfaces, so a short-lived bugfix/anti-diagonal branch is created off dev to fix it. When development is done, dev is merged into master so that master ends up fully synced with dev. Work through the scenario on your own machine using two clones (Repo1 = Alice, Repo2 = Ben), and fill in the Git command(s) and non-Git operations for every step.

The two functions you'll add

Add these at the top of tictactoe.py and call them from the game loop (after placing a mark: if check_win is true announce the winner and stop; else if board_full is true announce a draw and stop). Paste them exactly as shown, including Alice's bug, which you'll hunt down later.

# Alice's feature: True if player p holds a full row, column, or diagonal.
def check_win(b, p):
    lines = [
        (0,1,2), (3,4,5), (6,7,8),   # rows
        (0,3,6), (1,4,7), (2,5,8),   # columns
        (0,4,8), (2,4,8),            # diagonals
    ]
    for line in lines:
        if b[line[0]] == p and b[line[1]] == p and b[line[2]] == p:
            return True
    return False
# Ben's feature: True once every cell holds a mark (no '1'..'9' left).
def board_full(b):
    for c in b:
        if c != 'X' and c != 'O':
            return False
    return True

# tictactoe.py: end state (win + draw detection, bug fixed)

def check_win(b, p):
    lines = [
        (0,1,2), (3,4,5), (6,7,8),
        (0,3,6), (1,4,7), (2,5,8),
        (0,4,8), (2,4,6),            # anti-diagonal fixed
    ]
    for line in lines:
        if b[line[0]] == p and b[line[1]] == p and b[line[2]] == p:
            return True
    return False


def board_full(b):
    for c in b:
        if c != 'X' and c != 'O':
            return False
    return True


board = ['1', '2', '3', '4', '5', '6', '7', '8', '9']
player = 'X'


def draw():
    for r in range(3):
        print(f" {board[r*3]}|{board[r*3+1]}|{board[r*3+2]}")


while True:
    draw()
    cell = input(f"Player {player}, cell 1-9: ")
    if not cell.isdigit() or not (1 <= int(cell) <= 9) or board[int(cell)-1] in ('X', 'O'):
        print("invalid")
        continue
    board[int(cell) - 1] = player
    if check_win(board, player):
        draw()
        print(f"Player {player} wins!")
        break
    if board_full(board):
        draw()
        print("Draw")
        break
    player = 'O' if player == 'X' else 'X'

Module 5 · Lecture · Class 9

Testing with pytest

Write small checks that prove your code behaves, and run them all with one command.

Until now you've tested by hand: run the program, type some moves, eyeball the output. That doesn't scale: it's slow, easy to skip, and a fix in one place can silently break another. Automated tests are small programs that check your code for you, in seconds, every time. pytest is the tool that finds and runs them.

1 · Why automated tests

Manual testing has three problems: it's slow, it gets skipped when you're in a hurry, and it misses regressions: a change that quietly breaks something that used to work. An automated test pins down one expected behaviour once; from then on, every time you change the code, the test tells you in seconds whether you broke it.

  • The anti-diagonal bug from Lab 3 (cells 3-5-7 not detected) is exactly the kind of thing a single test would have caught the moment it was introduced.
  • Tests double as documentation: they show, in code, how a function is meant to be used.
  • They are a safety net for refactoring: change the insides freely, and if the tests still pass, the behaviour is intact.
  • The payoff compounds in Module 6, where the CI pipeline runs your tests automatically on every push.

2 · Make code testable: separate logic from I/O

A test calls your code and checks what comes back. It can't easily "type into" an input() prompt or read what print() put on screen. The fix is to keep the decisions and rules (pure logic) in functions that take arguments and return values, separate from the input()/print() that talk to the user.

Take the hello project. Instead of one script that prints directly, move the logic into a function that returns a string:

# greeter.py: pure logic, no I/O
def greet(name):
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

The I/O (asking for a name, printing the result) lives elsewhere. Now greet() is trivially testable: hand it a name, check the string it returns. A function that returns a value is easy to test; a function that only prints is not.

3 · Organise the project: src/ and tests/

So far everything has lived in one folder. As a project grows, that gets crowded: source files, test files, and generated junk all jumbled together. The common convention is to give each a home: application code in a src/ folder, tests in a tests/ folder.

hello/
├── src/
│   └── greeter.py       # the code under test
├── tests/
│   └── test_greeter.py  # the tests
└── pyproject.toml       # tells pytest where the code lives

There's one catch: once greeter.py moves into src/, the line from greeter import greet can no longer find it: src/ isn't on Python's import path. Rather than set PYTHONPATH by hand every time, add a small pyproject.toml at the project root and let pytest handle it:

# pyproject.toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
pythonpath = ["src"]

That one setting tells pytest to add src/ to the import path before it runs, so your tests keep writing from greeter import greet unchanged. The file also marks the project root, so pytest discovers the same tests/ no matter which sub-folder you launch it from.

4 · Writing and running a test

pytest discovers tests by name: files called test_*.py and functions called test_*. A test calls the function and asserts the result is what you expect:

# test_greeter.py
from greeter import greet

def test_greet_uses_the_name():
    result = greet("world")            # Act
    assert result == "Hello, world!"    # Assert

Every test follows the same three beats: Arrange a situation, Act by calling the code, Assert the result. The assert is plain Python: if its expression is false, the test fails. To run every test in the project, go to the project root (the folder with pyproject.toml) and just type:

pytest

pytest reads pyproject.toml, puts src/ on the import path, then finds and runs every test_*.py under tests/; you never name the files yourself. A passing run is green; each dot is one passing test:

tests/test_greeter.py .                              [100%]

1 passed in 0.01s

If you break it (say greet returns "Hi, {name}"), pytest shows an F and (because it rewrites assert statements) the actual vs. expected values, so you see why it failed:

tests/test_greeter.py F                              [100%]

    def test_greet_uses_the_name():
        result = greet("world")
>       assert result == "Hello, world!"
E       AssertionError: assert 'Hi, world' == 'Hello, world!'

1 failed in 0.02s

Add pytest -v for a verbose list of each test by name.

5 · Cover the cases

Good tests check the happy path and the edges. Give each behaviour its own test_ function and name it so a failure reads like a sentence (test_greet_handles_empty_name). When several cases differ only in their inputs, don't copy-paste; parametrize one test to run once per row:

import pytest
from greeter import greet

@pytest.mark.parametrize("name, expected", [
    ("world", "Hello, world!"),
    ("Sam",   "Hello, Sam!"),
    ("",      "Hello, !"),
])
def test_greet(name, expected):
    assert greet(name) == expected

pytest runs this test three times, reporting each row separately, so one failing case doesn't hide the others.

6 · The exit code (why CI cares)

When it finishes, pytest returns an exit code: 0 if every test passed, non-zero if any failed. That single number is the signal the CI pipeline watches in Module 6: green when it's 0, red otherwise. The pipeline runs the very same pytest command you run locally, on a clean machine.

On to the lab

In Lab 4 you'll make the Tic-Tac-Toe rules testable by moving them into a Board class, then write pytest tests for it, including a regression test for the Lab 3 anti-diagonal bug. In Module 6, Gitee Go runs pytest automatically on every push.

Lab 4: Test the Game

Make the game's rules testable, then write a pytest suite that proves they work.

1 · Make the logic testable

To test the rules, they must be callable without running the input loop. Split the single tictactoe.py into two files: the logic in a Board class (no I/O), and the game loop that uses it. Then organise the project into src/ and tests/ as you saw in the lecture:

tictactoe/
├── src/
│   ├── board.py        # the rules: a Board class, no input/print (given)
│   └── tictactoe.py    # the game loop, imports Board (given)
├── tests/
│   └── test_board.py   # YOUR pytest tests (Section 2)
└── pyproject.toml      # tells pytest where the code lives

The pyproject.toml at the root puts src/ on the import path, so the imports below stay simple (from board import Board) even though the code now lives in a sub-folder:

# pyproject.toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
pythonpath = ["src"]

board.py holds the pure logic, with the anti-diagonal bug already fixed:

# board.py - pure game logic, no I/O
class Board:
    def __init__(self):
        self.cells = ['1', '2', '3', '4', '5', '6', '7', '8', '9']

    def is_valid_move(self, cell):
        return 1 <= cell <= 9 and self.cells[cell - 1] not in ('X', 'O')

    def apply_move(self, cell, player):
        self.cells[cell - 1] = player

    def is_full(self):
        return all(c in ('X', 'O') for c in self.cells)

    def winner(self):
        lines = [
            (0, 1, 2), (3, 4, 5), (6, 7, 8),
            (0, 3, 6), (1, 4, 7), (2, 5, 8),
            (0, 4, 8), (2, 4, 6),
        ]
        for a, b, c in lines:
            if self.cells[a] in ('X', 'O') and self.cells[a] == self.cells[b] == self.cells[c]:
                return self.cells[a]
        return ' '

    def cell_mark(self, cell):
        return self.cells[cell - 1]

tictactoe.py is the input/output, importing Board. The if __name__ == "__main__" guard means importing this file does not start the game (so it never blocks a test):

# tictactoe.py - the game's input/output, using the Board logic
from board import Board


def draw(board):
    for r in range(3):
        print(f" {board.cell_mark(r*3+1)}|{board.cell_mark(r*3+2)}|{board.cell_mark(r*3+3)}")


def main():
    board = Board()
    player = 'X'
    while True:
        draw(board)
        cell = input(f"Player {player}, cell 1-9: ")
        if not cell.isdigit() or not board.is_valid_move(int(cell)):
            print("invalid")
            continue
        board.apply_move(int(cell), player)
        if board.winner() != ' ':
            draw(board)
            print(f"Player {player} wins!")
            break
        if board.is_full():
            draw(board)
            print("Draw")
            break
        player = 'O' if player == 'X' else 'X'


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

2 · Write your own tests

Create test_board.py in tests/ and write pytest tests for the Board class, modelled on the lecture (Class 9). Don't copy a finished file: build it from the requirements below. Two tests are given to show the shape: arrange a board with apply_move, then assert on winner() / is_full() / is_valid_move():

# test_board.py
from board import Board


def test_row_win():
    b = Board()
    b.apply_move(1, 'X'); b.apply_move(2, 'X'); b.apply_move(3, 'X')
    assert b.winner() == 'X'


def test_anti_diagonal_win():   # regression test for the Lab 3 bug
    b = Board()
    b.apply_move(3, 'X'); b.apply_move(5, 'X'); b.apply_move(7, 'X')
    assert b.winner() == 'X'
Your suite must also test
  1. A column win (e.g. O on cells 1, 4, 7) is detected.
  2. No winner yet: a board with a couple of moves returns ' ' from winner().
  3. A full board makes is_full() return True (and an empty one returns False).
  4. Move validation: is_valid_move rejects a taken cell and an out-of-range cell (0 or 10), and accepts a free one.

Module 6 · Lecture · Class 11

Pipeline Configuration

What a pipeline is, how it is built from stages and steps, and how to write one in YAML for Gitee Go.

You can already run your tests with one command, pytest. A pipeline hands that command (and more) to a server so it runs automatically on every change, on a clean machine. This is the engine of CI/CD: Continuous Integration tests every change as it arrives, and Continuous Delivery packages the verified result so it is ready to ship. We build one on Gitee with Gitee Go.

1 · What is a pipeline?

A pipeline is an automated, ordered sequence of work that runs whenever the repository changes. Every push (or Pull Request) triggers it; it checks out the new commit on a fresh machine, runs your build, tests, and delivery, and reports green (all good) or red (something failed). Because it runs on a clean machine every time, it catches "works on my machine" problems and stops broken code from reaching master.

Our pipeline has three phases. Gitee Go draws it left to right like this:

           ┌─ Compile ───────────┐     ┌─ Test ──────────────┐     ┌─ Publish ───────┐
 push ──▶   │  • Python Build     │ ──▶ │  • Python Unit Tests│ ──▶ │  • Publish      │
           │  • Upload Artifact  │     │                     │     │                 │
           └─────────────────────┘     └─────────────────────┘     └─────────────────┘
            steps run in order          runs if Compile passed      runs if Test passed

It reads like a sentence: compile the project and save the result, test it, and only if that passes, publish a release.

2 · Anatomy: stages, steps, and tasks

A pipeline is built from three nested pieces:

  • A stage is a major phase, drawn as one column above (Compile, Test, Publish). Stages run in order and are fail-fast: if one fails, the pipeline stops and the stages after it never run. That ordering is what makes Test a gate before Publish.
  • A step is one box inside a stage (Python Build, Upload Artifact, …). A stage runs its steps top to bottom. Compile above has two steps; Test has one.
  • A task (Gitee calls it a plugin) is what a step actually does: "run Python commands", "run unit tests", "publish a release", and so on. In the YAML a step names its task with step: build@python, step: ut@python, or step: publish@release_artifacts.

So the hierarchy is pipeline → stages → steps → one task each. Steps can also hand data forward: the Upload Artifact step saves the project as an artifact that the Publish stage later releases.

"Compile" for Python?

Python isn't compiled to a machine-code binary, but the Compile stage still earns its name: python3 -m compileall src byte-compiles every file in src/, which fails fast on any syntax error before a single test runs. The stage also installs dependencies and packages the source as an artifact.

3 · YAML in sixty seconds

Gitee Go stores the pipeline as a YAML file. YAML is a plain-text format for configuration, built from key: value pairs. Three rules cover almost everything:

  • Indentation shows nesting (spaces only, never tabs): a key indented under another belongs to it.
  • A leading - makes a list item.
  • # starts a comment; blank lines are ignored.
name: master-pipeline        # a key and its (string) value
pythonVersion: '3.13'        # quotes keep it a string, not the number 3.13
stages:                      # this key's value is a list…
  - name: test               # "-" starts one list item (itself a mapping)
    steps:                   # nested under this stage
      - pip install pytest   # a list of two commands
      - pytest

Values are usually unquoted; quote one to keep it a string (so '3.13' isn't read as a number and '1.0' keeps its trailing zero). That is enough YAML to read and edit any pipeline.

4 · The pipeline file, explained

Here is the real pipeline file behind that diagram: Gitee's Python template, filled in for our project. (Gitee's editor also writes a few empty default fields such as executor: [], checkpoints: [], caches: [] and notify: []; they're trimmed here, so just leave them as the editor wrote them.)

# .workflow/master-pipeline.yml
version: '1.0'
name: master-pipeline
displayName: MasterPipeline
triggers:                              # WHEN it runs: automatically, on push to master
  trigger: auto
  push:
    branches:
      include:
        - master
stages:
  - name: compile                      # Stage 1: install deps, byte-compile, package
    displayName: Compile
    strategy: naturally                # run this stage's steps in order
    trigger: auto
    steps:
      - step: build@python             # task: a Python 3.13 environment
        name: build_python
        displayName: Python Build
        pythonVersion: '3.13'
        commands:
          - python3 -m pip install --upgrade pip
          - pip3 config set global.index-url https://pypi.tuna.tsinghua.edu.cn/simple   # China mirror
          - pip3 install -r requirements.txt
          - python3 -m compileall src   # byte-compile src/ (fails on a syntax error)
        artifacts:                      # capture the project as an artifact…
          - name: BUILD_ARTIFACT
            path:
              - ./
      - step: publish@general_artifacts # task: save that artifact as "output"
        name: publish_general_artifacts
        displayName: Upload Artifact
        dependArtifact: BUILD_ARTIFACT
        artifactName: output
        dependsOn: build_python
  - name: test                         # Stage 2: the CI gate
    displayName: Test
    strategy: naturally
    trigger: auto
    steps:
      - step: ut@python                # task: unit tests + a test report
        name: unit_test_python
        displayName: Python Unit Tests
        pythonVersion: '3.13'
        commands:
          - pip3 config set global.index-url https://pypi.tuna.tsinghua.edu.cn/simple
          - pip3 install -r requirements.txt
          - pytest --html=report/index.html   # run tests, write an HTML report
        report:                         # surface that report on the run page
          path: report
          index: index.html
  - name: release                      # Stage 3: CD, only if Test passed
    displayName: Publish
    strategy: naturally
    trigger: auto
    steps:
      - step: publish@release_artifacts
        name: publish_release_artifacts
        displayName: Publish
        dependArtifact: output
        version: 1.0.0.0
        autoIncrement: true            # bump the version each release
  • version / name / displayName: the file-format version, the pipeline's id, and the label shown in the UI.
  • triggers says when it runs: trigger: auto + push.branches.include: [master] means "automatically, on any push to master." (Add a pull_request trigger to gate merges too.)
  • strategy: naturally runs a stage's steps in their listed order. Stages themselves run top-to-bottom and fail-fast.
  • step: picks the task: build@python runs commands in a Python 3.13 environment, ut@python runs unit tests and captures a report, and publish@general_artifacts / publish@release_artifacts handle the artifact and the release.
  • commands: the Compile step upgrades pip, points it at the Tsinghua mirror (fast from China), installs requirements.txt, then python3 -m compileall src byte-compiles your code (a free syntax check before any test runs).
  • report: the Test step runs pytest --html=report/index.html, and the report: block surfaces that HTML report on the run page, so you can browse failures without scrolling the raw log.
  • dependsOn / dependArtifact: order steps and pass the saved output artifact from Upload Artifact through to Publish.

5 · Three pipelines: master, branch, and PR

The file above is the master pipeline: it triggers on a push to master. But work at different points needs different treatment, so Gitee Go lets you configure three pipelines, each with its own trigger:

PipelineTriggered when…Typical stages
Mastera push or merge lands on masterCompile → Test → Publish
Branchyou push to a feature branch (not master)Compile → Test
PRa Pull Request targeting master is opened or updatedCompile → Test (the merge gate)
  • Only the master pipeline publishes. You release from master because that's the finished, reviewed line; the branch and PR pipelines stop at Test; you don't ship unfinished or unreviewed work.
  • The branch pipeline gives you fast feedback while you develop on a feature branch: every push builds and tests your work-in-progress, so you catch breakage early.
  • The PR pipeline is the merge gate from Module 4: it runs build + test against the proposed merge, and a red result blocks the Pull Request from being merged, so broken code never reaches master.

It's the same building blocks (stages, steps, tasks) each time; only the trigger and whether there's a Publish stage differ. Our file's triggers: push: branches: include: [master] is what makes it the master pipeline; a branch pipeline would list other branches, and a PR pipeline uses a pull_request trigger.

6 · Run it on Gitee, red then green

  1. In your repo, open the Services (服务) tab → enable Gitee Go, and Create pipeline from the Python template (which gives you exactly the Compile / Test / Publish shape above). Gitee saves it under .workflow/ in your repo.
  2. Commit & push, then watch it run: green when pytest passes, red when it fails (with the failing assertion in the logs).
  3. Break a test on purpose to see Test go red and Publish skipped; fix it to go green.

Because Test sits before Publish and stages are fail-fast, a failing test blocks the release; that is the whole point. The Publish stage is the CD half: it publishes a tested, versioned release with no manual steps.

Module 6 · Lab 5 · Class 12

Lab 5: Test Pipeline on Gitee Go

Automate your pytest suite, then drive a change through the branch, PR, and master pipelines.

This lab uses the tested project from Lab 4 (src/board.py, src/tictactoe.py, and your tests/test_board.py). You'll put pytest behind automated pipelines and watch all three pipeline types from Class 11 fire.

1 · Confirm the tests pass locally

From the project root, make sure the suite is green before automating it; the pipeline can only run what already works on your machine:

pytest

If pytest isn't found, install it with pip install pytest (see Module 1). Record the test dependencies so the pipeline installs the same ones: create a requirements.txt. The pipeline writes an HTML test report, which needs the pytest-html plugin:

# requirements.txt
pytest
pytest-html

2 · Set up the three pipelines

Enable Gitee Go on your repo (the Services tab). You'll create three pipelines under .workflow/, one per trigger type from Class 11. Start with the master pipeline: create a pipeline from the Python template and replace it with the file below, the three-stage Compile → Test → Publish file (see Class 11 for a key-by-key explanation):

# .workflow/master-pipeline.yml
version: '1.0'
name: master-pipeline
displayName: MasterPipeline
triggers:
  trigger: auto
  push:
    branches:
      include:
        - master
stages:
  - name: compile
    displayName: Compile
    strategy: naturally
    trigger: auto
    steps:
      - step: build@python
        name: build_python
        displayName: Python Build
        pythonVersion: '3.13'
        commands:
          - python3 -m pip install --upgrade pip
          - pip3 config set global.index-url https://pypi.tuna.tsinghua.edu.cn/simple
          - pip3 install -r requirements.txt
          - python3 -m compileall src
        artifacts:
          - name: BUILD_ARTIFACT
            path:
              - ./
      - step: publish@general_artifacts
        name: publish_general_artifacts
        displayName: Upload Artifact
        dependArtifact: BUILD_ARTIFACT
        artifactName: output
        dependsOn: build_python
  - name: test
    displayName: Test
    strategy: naturally
    trigger: auto
    executor: []
    steps:
      - step: ut@python
        name: unit_test_python
        displayName: Python Unit Tests
        pythonVersion: '3.13'
        commands:
          - pip3 config set global.index-url https://pypi.tuna.tsinghua.edu.cn/simple
          - pip3 install -r requirements.txt
          - pytest --html=report/index.html
        report:
          path: report
          index: index.html
        checkpoints: []
        caches: []
        notify: []
        strategy:
          retry: '0'
  - name: release
    displayName: Publish
    strategy: naturally
    trigger: auto
    steps:
      - step: publish@release_artifacts
        name: publish_release_artifacts
        displayName: Publish
        dependArtifact: output
        version: 1.0.0.0
        autoIncrement: true
        strategy: {}

This is the real file from Gitee's Python template; the empty fields (executor, checkpoints, caches, notify, strategy) are editor defaults you can leave as-is.

Now add a branch pipeline and a PR pipeline. Both are copies of the master pipeline with the release (Publish) stage removed (you don't publish from unmerged work) and a different trigger. When you create each one in Gitee Go, pick its trigger type and Gitee writes the matching triggers block:

# branch pipeline: fires on a push to any non-master branch (Compile + Test, no Publish)
triggers:
  trigger: auto
  push:
    branches:
      exclude:
        - master
# PR pipeline: fires when a Pull Request targets master (Compile + Test, no Publish)
triggers:
  trigger: auto
  pr:
    branches:
      include:
        - master

The exact trigger keys come from the Gitee Go editor when you choose a pipeline's trigger type (master branch / regular branch / pull request); keep the shape: branch and PR pipelines run Compile + Test, never Publish.

3 · Exercise the branch pipeline: red, then green

  1. Create a dev branch off master and switch to it: git switch -c dev.
  2. Make a small change on dev that introduces a bug one of your tests catches: for example, in src/board.py change the anti-diagonal line back to (2, 4, 8), so test_anti_diagonal_win will fail. Commit and push the branch: git push -u origin dev.
  3. On Gitee, watch the branch pipeline run and turn red. Open the failed Test stage and read the failing assertion in the HTML report.
  4. Fix the bug (restore (2, 4, 6)), commit, and push again. The branch pipeline re-runs and turns green.

4 · Open a PR (PR pipeline), then merge (master pipeline)

  1. On Gitee, open a Pull Request from dev into master. The PR pipeline runs against the proposed merge; confirm it is green (a red PR pipeline blocks the merge).
  2. Merge the PR. The push to master triggers the master pipeline: Compile → Test → Publish, which publishes a versioned release.
  3. Tidy up: delete the dev branch (Gitee's button after the merge, and git branch -d dev locally).
Submit

A screenshot of all three pipelines' run history: the branch pipeline showing a red run followed by a green run, the PR pipeline's green run, and the master pipeline's green run that published the release.

Done when

All three pipelines exist and have fired: the branch pipeline went red then green, the PR pipeline gated the merge, and merging ran the master pipeline through to a published release.

Module 7 · Capstone · Final Project

Final Project

In teams, extend the game through the full workflow you've learned: from issue to released, tested code.

Everything so far has built the machinery: version control, a clean repo, branches, automated tests, and a CI/CD pipeline. Now you put it to work. In teams of 2–3, add one feature to Tic-Tac-Toe and take it through the complete professional loop.

Schedule

PlanDiscussion & planning. Form teams, choose a feature, open issues on Gitee, assign owners, plan branches, agree on "done."
BuildImplementation. Issue-driven development: branch per issue → code + a unit test → push → PR → CI gate → review → merge.
DemoIntegration & demo. Final merge to master and present.

Choose a feature

EasyRandom-move AI

A single-player mode where the computer plays a random legal move.

HardUnbeatable AI (minimax)

An opponent that never loses, and is very testable ("must take a winning move," "must never lose").

MediumN×N board

Generalise the board and win logic to larger sizes / Connect-Four style.

MediumScore & replay

A persistent high-score file and a play-again loop with difficulty levels.

Follow Git Flow

Professional teams don't commit straight to the main line; they follow a branching model. The most common is Git Flow: two long-lived branches (main and develop) plus short-lived feature, release, and hotfix branches that each have one job. For this project, develop your feature using this flow.

Each branch has one job:

  • main: always-releasable history; here it's your repo's default branch (master on Gitee).
  • develop: the integration branch where finished features come together.
  • feature/<name>: one per issue, branched off develop and merged back via a Pull Request once CI is green. This is where your team's work happens.
  • release/*: a stabilising branch cut from develop when you're ready to ship; merges into main and back into develop.
  • hotfix/*: an urgent fix branched off main and merged back into both main and develop.
Do this

Develop your feature on a feature/<name> branch off develop, open a PR back into develop once the pipeline is green, and keep master for integrated, releasable code. Never commit straight to master.

Definition of done

  • The feature works and is merged into master via a Pull Request.
  • It has at least one meaningful unit test for any new logic.
  • CI (Gitee Go) is green on master.
  • The work is traceable: issues linked to PRs.

Assessment rubric

CriterionWeight
Working feature, merged to master30%
At least one meaningful unit test20%
CI pipeline passing on master20%
Clean issue → branch → PR history showing the workflow20%
Clear demo of the working feature10%
Demo

Each team shows: the green pipeline, the issue→PR history, and the feature played live. Close with a one-minute reflection on what branching and CI saved you.
